content.text: Imbalanced data makes accuracy useless and a 0.5 cutoff look broken, but neither means you must rebalance the data. Measure how well the model ranks positives with a threshold-free metric, then choose the decision threshold for the mistakes you care about. In a large benchmark, balancing didn't help strong classifiers, and tuning the threshold matched it on label metrics such as F1.

A payments team trains a gradient-boosted classifier on transactions where about 2% are fraud. Accuracy: 0.979. Then someone checks recall and finds the model catches 14% of the fraud. The next ticket reads "Add SMOTE to fix the imbalance." Before anyone generates a single synthetic row, the same model with a different cutoff catches 49%.
Many developers assume an imbalanced dataset must be rebalanced, usually with SMOTE, before training. It's easy to see why:

items.text: SMOTE is everywhere. The paper behind this article counts 156 Google Scholar papers with "SMOTE" in the title in 2021 alone, and more than 100 published variants.
The symptom seems to point there: the model predicts almost no positives, so it looks like it never saw enough of them.
Rebalancing really does help in some setups, such as weak classifiers or a cutoff you can't change, so success stories are real.

content.text: The half-truth: rebalancing changes what the model outputs at a cutoff of 0.5. Moving the cutoff does that too, it costs nothing, and it leaves the training data alone.
An imbalanced problem has two separate questions: how well does the model rank risky cases above safe ones, and where do you draw the line? The 0.5 default answers the second one for you, badly.

, accuracy rewards ignoring the rare class. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course says accuracy is usually a poor metric for imbalanced datasets: if 1% of examples are positive, a model that always predicts negative scores 99% and is useless. The script shows the same with a 2% positive class.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=8000, n_features=10, n_informative=4,
                           weights=[0.98], random_state=0)  # ~2% positive
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
models = {"always negative": DummyClassifier(),
          "boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)}
for name, model in models.items():
    pred = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
    print(f"{name:<15} accuracy {accuracy_score(y_te, pred):.3f}"
          f"  recall {recall_score(y_te, pred):.3f}")
# always negative accuracy 0.976  recall 0.000
# boosting        accuracy 0.979  recall 0.143
# "It misses most positives: rebalance the data with SMOTE"

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, f1_score, recall_score
from sklearn.model_selection import TunedThresholdClassifierCV, train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=8000, n_features=10, n_informative=4,
                           weights=[0.98], random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
hgb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
ap = average_precision_score(y_te, hgb.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1])
print(f"average precision {ap:.3f}")  # ranking quality, no threshold involved
for name, model in [
    ("threshold 0.5", hgb),
    ("tuned threshold", TunedThresholdClassifierCV(hgb, scoring="f1")),
    ("balanced weights", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        class_weight="balanced", random_state=0)),
]:
    pred = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
    cut = getattr(model, "best_threshold_", 0.5)
    print(f"{name:<16} cutoff {cut:.3f}  F1 {f1_score(y_te, pred):.3f}"
          f"  recall {recall_score(y_te, pred):.3f}")
# average precision 0.439
# threshold 0.5    cutoff 0.500  F1 0.250  recall 0.143
# tuned threshold  cutoff 0.029  F1 0.444  recall 0.490
# balanced weights cutoff 0.500  F1 0.442  recall 0.347

content.text: The boosted model beats "always negative" by 0.003 of accuracy, which says nothing. Recall, the share of real positives it catches, is the number that exposes the problem: 0.143.
A classifier outputs a score, not a verdict

of 0.5. When positives are 2% of the data, a transaction with a 20% fraud probability is ten times riskier than average and still gets labeled "legitimate". Low recall at 0.5 tells you the cutoff is wrong for this problem. It doesn't tell you the model failed to learn.

Average precision summarizes precision across every possible threshold, so it judges the scores themselves. scikit-learn's precision-recall example calls this family of measures useful when classes are very imbalanced. Here it is 0.439, where a random ranking would score about the positive rate, roughly 0.02. The model has learned a lot; the cutoff was hiding it.

picks the threshold that maximizes a metric, using an internal stratified 5-fold cross-validation by default. Optimizing F1, it lands on 0.029: F1 rises from 0.250 to 0.444 and recall from 0.143 to 0.490, at the price of more false alarms, which is the trade the Crash Course describes for any lower threshold.
, which reweights the classes instead of resampling them, reaches about the same F1, 0.442, with a different mix of recall and precision.

Elor and Averbuch-Elor tested balancing on dozens of imbalanced tabular datasets with LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost alongside weaker learners. On probability metrics such as AUC, balancing helped the weaker classifiers but not the strongest, XGBoost and CatBoost, and strong classifiers without balancing beat weak ones with it. On label metrics such as F1, balancing and threshold optimization gave similar results, and the authors recommend the threshold because the model is trained once. When they did balance, plain random oversampling was as effective as SMOTE-like methods.

blocks.title: Put the business cost in the metric

content.text: F1 is a stand-in. If a missed fraud costs far more than a false alarm, give
that reflects those costs; scikit-learn has a worked example of post-tuning the threshold for cost-sensitive learning.

blocks.title: Keep the test data out of both fixes

content.text: The scikit-learn guide is explicit: never use the same data to train the classifier and tune its threshold. The same logic applies to resampling. Oversample the full dataset before splitting and copies or interpolations of test rows land in training, so the score is inflated. Resample only inside the training folds.

blocks.title: One kind of resampling with a different job

content.text: Google's Crash Course does recommend resampling for a training problem, not an evaluation one. With 200 majority and 2 minority examples, a batch of 100 holds on average a single minority example. Its fix is to downsample the majority class and upweight it by the same factor: the model sees the rare class more often and converges faster, and the upweighting corrects the prediction bias that downsampling alone would introduce.

items.text: On imbalanced data, accuracy rewards ignoring the rare class: "always negative" scored 0.976.
Low recall at a 0.5 cutoff is usually a threshold problem; the same model went from 0.143 to 0.490 recall.
Judge the ranking with a threshold-free metric, then set the threshold from the costs of each mistake.
Rebalancing, SMOTE included, didn't help strong classifiers in a large benchmark; use it with evidence, not by default.
